overview: This record follows independent Côte d’Ivoire, also called Ivory Coast in English, from 1960. Independence ended French sovereignty; it did not begin the histories of the many communities living within the new state.

periods.title: Independence and the republic
periods.summary: Côte d’Ivoire became independent on 7 August 1960.

periods.title: Conflict and peacekeeping
periods.summary: A UN mission supported the peace process and later addressed the crisis following the 2010 election.

periods.title: After the peacekeeping mission
periods.summary: UNOCI closed in June 2017; the country continued as an independent state.

items.text: On 7 August 1960, the country gained independence from France. That same day, an American recognition letter went to Félix Houphouët-Boigny and the US consulate in Abidjan became an embassy: diplomatic paperwork provides a dated trail of the new republic entering international relations.

Here is a short writing sample from Article 1 of the November 1960 constitution: “Union, Discipline, Travail.” In English, this French motto means “Unity, Discipline, Work.” The document also named French as the official language; this state text does not represent all the languages spoken at home.

Peacekeeping was part of a difficult political recovery. The UN created UNOCI in 2004 to help implement a peace agreement. After the disputed 2010 presidential election, violence escalated when Laurent Gbagbo refused to leave office following the UN-certified victory of Alassane Ouattara; Ouattara was inaugurated in May 2011.

Attiéké begins as cassava rather than wheat. Producers grind the tubers, mix them with fermented cassava, turn the mixture into small grains and steam it. The cooled food can be packed in baskets lined with cassava leaves: a whole sequence of skilled work sits behind a seemingly simple plate.

UNESCO’s account describes women preparing, preserving and selling attiéké, while men contribute to cultivation, harvesting, transport and grinding. Knowledge passes through watching, doing and spoken instruction within families. Learning to make dinner can also mean learning a business.

Attiéké connects ordinary meals with public occasions. It appears at home, in restaurants, at weddings and other gatherings. Its affordability helps explain its wide use, while production and sales provide income, especially for women.

Among Guro communities around Bouaflé and Zuénoula, a Zaouli performance joins several arts: a carved mask, woven costume, music, singing and fast-moving dance. The dancer is the most visible participant, but sculptors, textile workers and musicians help make the performance possible.

Zaouli is learned through people as well as objects. Experienced performers teach younger participants during lessons and performances, while festivals and dance competitions bring communities together. UNESCO’s account identifies seven mask types, each associated with a legend: a mask carries a story as well as a face.

In UNICEF’s account of a 2018 Gonzagueville pilot, Adja, a mother of three, earned money collecting discarded plastic. Unpredictable prices sometimes left her storing sacks at home. Recycling therefore involved family income and working conditions, as well as getting rubbish out of streets.

That pilot classroom used interlocking recycled-plastic bricks developed by the Colombian enterprise Conceptos Plasticos. The imported bricks were assembled in five days with a hammer, rather like an enormous construction toy. The report expected forty kindergarten pupils when term began; wider local production was still a future plan.

In 2024, UNICEF reported replacing worn-out hand-powered pumps in nineteen Bounkani villages, improving drinking-water access for roughly 7,600 people. A functioning pump is an unglamorous achievement with a very practical audience: everyone carrying the next bucket.

School hygiene needs maintenance as much as construction. The same 2024 report describes training 148 school principals and supervisors in Bouna and Ferkessedougou. Activities covered handwashing, wastewater, rubbish and toilet upkeep. A toilet is only useful if someone keeps it usable.

ending.text: The republic did not end with its civil conflicts. UNOCI closed on 30 June 2017 after completing its mandate, while state institutions and community life continued. The mission’s departure marks a change in international support, not the disappearance of Côte d’Ivoire.
